h: A museum in a park, and a park with Highland cows
p: Part of the joy of the Burrell is the building itself. Opened in 1983, it was designed so the art sits alongside the landscape, with huge glass walls looking straight out into the woodland. On a bright day, sunlight pours across stone doorways and sculpture, and it feels more like walking through the trees than round a gallery. The refurbished building has extra gallery space and a lot more of Burrell's collection on show than before.

Allow two to three hours, and don't be afraid to pace yourself. The variety is such that it's easy to get overwhelmed, so pick a few galleries that grab you and come back another time for the rest. As entry is free, that's an easy promise to keep.

Make sure you leave time for Pollok Country Park itself, Glasgow's biggest park and a brilliant place for a walk. Look out for the herd of Highland cattle grazing in the fields, which are always a hit with kids and visitors from abroad. There are woodland trails, gardens and space for a picnic when the weather plays ball.

Just a short walk away is Pollok House, an elegant 18th-century mansion cared for by the National Trust for Scotland. It's famous as the place where the idea for the National Trust for Scotland was first discussed, and it has its own art collection and an Edwardian kitchen café, making it a perfect add-on.
The park is easy to reach by train, with Pollokshaws West station close to the park's edge, and buses run from the city centre.
